passage: In the small town of Malegaon, Asif, twenty, counted every coin of his daily money. He walked three kilometres to college to save the ten-rupee shared auto, and he told Karthik, his friend from the repair shop where they both worked evenings, that chai at the stall was a luxury. Then the shop owner gave them each an Eid bonus of four thousand rupees. Asif spent his in a week: a big speaker, biryani for six friends, and a day trip to the dam on hired bikes. "Bonus money," he said. "It's extra." In March the exam form fee came due. Asif stood at the college window eight hundred rupees short and borrowed from Karthik, who had quietly kept his bonus aside.

qa.q: How far did Asif walk to college to save the auto fare?
qa.a: He walked three kilometres to save the ten-rupee shared auto.

qa.q: Why did spending the bonus in a week feel fine to Asif?
qa.a: He thought of it as "extra", separate from the daily money he guarded, so it didn't feel like part of his real budget.

qa.q: What could Asif try the next time a bonus arrives?
qa.a: He could look at all his money together, including coming costs like the exam fee, before deciding what the bonus is for.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel lending Asif money for the exam form?
qa.a: Karthik may be glad to help a friend but also a little surprised, having watched Asif fuss over ten-rupee autos and then spend a whole bonus in a week.

grounding: A young man pinches coins on daily costs but spends a bonus freely, and the separate mental pots leave him short when a fee comes due.

passage: In Lyon, Bao kept a tiny notebook of daily costs. He refused the coffee after lectures, carried his lunch in a jar and walked forty minutes to avoid buying a tram ticket. "Every cent counts," he told Ines. Then in June a tax refund of six hundred euros landed, from his part-time job at a bookshop. That wasn't in the notebook. By the end of the month it had become a weekend in Barcelona, a leather jacket and new headphones. "It's refund money," he said when Ines raised an eyebrow. "Free money." In August the rent went up, and the notebook showed Bao three hundred euros short. He stared at the neat list of saved coffees and felt foolish.

qa.q: How much was Bao's tax refund?
qa.a: A tax refund of six hundred euros.

qa.q: Why did Bao call the refund "free money"?
qa.a: It wasn't part of the notebook he tracked so carefully, so it felt separate from his real budget and easy to spend.

qa.q: What turning point shows Bao the problem, and what could he change?
qa.a: Finding himself short when the rent went up; he could put every euro, refunds included, into the same notebook so he sees the whole picture.

qa.q: What might Ines have been thinking on raising an eyebrow?
qa.a: Ines probably found it odd that someone who walked forty minutes to save a tram ticket would spend six hundred euros in a month.

grounding: A student saves small daily amounts but spends a tax refund carelessly, because keeping it in a separate mental account hides his whole situation.

passage:
On the first of every month, in his rented flat in Hyderabad's Kondapur, Vishal opened one spreadsheet. Top line: everything he had minus everything he owed. Below it: money in and money out for the last month. When his colleague Usha saw him doing it at lunch, she laughed. "You look like my grandfather."
"Your grandfather was probably right," Vishal said.
That month a bonus had arrived. Usha had already spent hers on a new phone. Vishal typed the bonus into the same sheet as his salary, not a separate one. "It's just money," he said. "Same as the rest." Then he moved part of it into two savings accounts he had named "Laptop" and "Visit Amma". "The names help me stick to goals," he told her. "But I always look at the total first."

qa.q: What was the top line of Vishal's spreadsheet?
qa.a: Everything he had minus everything he owed.

qa.q: Why did Vishal say "It's just money" about his bonus?
qa.a: He believes a bonus is no different from salary, so he wanted it counted in the whole picture rather than treated as a separate treat.

qa.q: Which of Vishal's habits keeps his labelled accounts helpful rather than misleading?
qa.a: Looking at the total first each month, so named accounts like "Laptop" serve his goals without hiding the full picture.

qa.q: How might Usha see Vishal's habit after spending her own bonus?
qa.a: She teased him at first, but she might start wondering whether seeing all her money in one place would help her too.

grounding: A young earner counts a bonus in the same pool as salary, tracks his total and monthly flow, and uses named accounts only as goal tools.

passage:
"So the wedding gift money goes in the 'fun' account, right?" Sachin asked, spreading the envelopes on the dining table.
"Wait," said Chandrika, his wife. "Before we label anything, let's see the whole picture. What do we have, what do we owe?"
"Why? Gift money is gift money."
"It's all our money. The gifts, your salary, my salary, the scooter loan. One list."
Sachin groaned but wrote it down. "Okay... that's less than I thought, once the loan's in."
"Right. And every month, what comes in and what goes out?"
"Now you sound like my father."
Chandrika laughed. "Then your father was clever. Now we label: 'Emergency', 'Goa in December', 'Fun'. Labels are for goals, not for pretending some rupees don't count."
Sachin picked up a pen. "Fine. But 'Fun' gets something."

qa.q: Where did Sachin want the wedding gift money to go?
qa.a: In the 'fun' account.

qa.q: Why did Sachin groan and then say "that's less than I thought"?
qa.a: He expected the gift money to feel like extra, but seeing the loan on the same list showed their real position, which surprised him.

qa.q: Which step did Chandrika insist on first, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Listing everything they had and owed in one place before labelling anything, so the labels serve goals instead of hiding what the money really is.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel about the talk once 'Fun' still gets something?
qa.a: He would probably feel respected rather than lectured, since his wish for fun stays in the plan while the whole picture comes first 🙂

grounding: A young wife treats all the couple's money as one pool, looks at what they own, owe and spend monthly, and only then uses labels for goals.

passage:
Monday: Before leaving for work, Manjula rattled off a list to Devika: "Feed the cat, lock the balcony door, take the milk packet in, finish the maths worksheet, call Nani at five, and don't open the door for anyone." When Manjula came home, the milk had curdled in the sun and the cat was yowling. Devika had remembered the worksheet and the door. That was all.
Wednesday: Devika looked miserable at breakfast. "I tried, Amma. It just fell out of my head." Manjula stirred her tea and thought about it.
Friday: This time Manjula stuck three short lines on the fridge: 1. Milk inside. 2. Feed cat. 3. Call Nani at five. "Tick each one." When she got home, all three had ticks in green crayon, and the cat was asleep on Devika's lap.

qa.q: What happened to the milk packet on Monday?
qa.a: The milk had curdled in the sun.

qa.q: How was Devika feeling when saying "It just fell out of my head"?
qa.a: Devika felt miserable and a bit ashamed, having really tried but still forgotten most of the long list 😔

qa.q: What change did Manjula make on Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: She put three short numbered steps on the fridge to tick, so Devika only had to hold a few things and could check them off.

qa.q: What might Manjula have thought on Monday when she came home?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated at first, finding sour milk and a hungry cat, and may have wondered whether Devika had listened at all.

grounding: A child given a long spoken list forgets most of it, then manages easily with three short written steps.

passage: Zeenat, don't cry over the forgotten eggs. Sit with your Tanuja Aunty for a minute. When I was nine, in Lucknow, my mother sent me to the bazaar with a list spoken very fast: "Tomatoes, coriander, green chillies, a packet of salt, soap, two candles, a matchbox, and ask the tailor if my blouse is ready." I repeated it all the way down the lane. At the shop I bought tomatoes and candles, and then my head was empty. I came home crying, just like you. My mother didn't scold. The next week she said, "Three things only. Say them back to me." Then three more on the next trip. Forty years of teaching, and I always told my students: small bundles, not one big sack. So, what were the three things your Ammi wanted today?

qa.q: What did young Tanuja manage to buy at the shop?
qa.a: Tomatoes and candles.

qa.q: How did young Tanuja feel walking home from the bazaar?
qa.a: She felt upset and helpless, crying because she had tried so hard to remember and her head had gone empty.

qa.q: What change did Tanuja's mother make, and why did it work?
qa.a: She gave only three things and asked Tanuja to say them back, so the list fit in a child's memory.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel hearing this story after forgetting the eggs?
qa.a: Zeenat might feel relieved and less ashamed, learning that a grown-up teacher once forgot a long list too.

grounding: An older neighbour recalls forgetting most of a long spoken shopping list as a child, and how three items at a time worked.

passage:
Tutor's note, Wednesday evening batch. Jeevan
Anirban (Class 10) sat through the whole revision hour on circle theorems with one earbud in, film songs leaking out, and his phone face up, lighting every few seconds with group messages. He nodded along and copied everything neatly. At the end I gave a five-question check. He got one right and said, "But I understood it while you were teaching, sir!" He looked genuinely confused.
What I did next: I asked him to try Friday's hour with the phone in my drawer and no music, just as an experiment. On Friday he fidgeted for ten minutes, then settled. He scored four out of five on a similar check and grinned. I've suggested he try the same at home and tell me how it goes.

qa.q: How many questions did Anirban get right on Wednesday's check?
qa.a: He got one right.

qa.q: Why was Anirban genuinely confused by his score?
qa.a: He felt he had understood while copying and nodding, not noticing that the songs and buzzing messages kept the ideas from sticking.

qa.q: What experiment did Jeevan suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Keeping the phone in the drawer and the music off for one hour; with fewer things pulling at his attention, the theorems stuck and he scored four.

qa.q: What might it be like for Jeevan to see Anirban grin on Friday?
qa.a: Jeevan would likely feel pleased and hopeful, having helped a student find this out through his own experiment instead of a scolding.

grounding: A tutor notes a teenager whose learning does not stick while music and a buzzing phone overload his attention, and how removing them helps.

passage:
Tuesday, 10:30 pm
Three hours on biology tonight. Photosynthesis. I had my playlist on, the one with the loud Tamil songs, and the class group was going crazy about the cricket match, so my phone buzzed every minute. I kept replying "lol" and reading the same paragraph about chlorophyll.
Just now Lalit called to quiz me for tomorrow's test. He asked, "What are the two stages?" Blank. Totally blank. I could remember every line of the song, though. Every line!
Lalit said, "Your brain is doing three jobs at once." Annoying, but maybe true.
Tomorrow morning: one hour, phone in Amma's room, no songs. Let's see.
Chaitanya

qa.q: What question did Lalit ask?
qa.a: "What are the two stages?"

qa.q: What does Chaitanya remembering every line of the song suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Chaitanya's attention was going to the music and messages rather than the biology, which is frustrating after three hours of trying 😅

qa.q: What plan does Chaitanya make, and why might it work?
qa.a: One hour in the morning with the phone in Amma's room and no songs; with fewer demands on attention, the biology has a better chance to stick.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel quizzing a friend who draws a blank?
qa.a: Lalit may be surprised and a little worried about the test, and cares enough to point out the problem even if it annoys.

grounding: A teenager studies for hours with loud songs and a buzzing phone and finds the biology did not stick.

passage:
Dear Francis,
Sorry I missed your birthday call. My brain is soup these days. Exams all month, evening shifts at the hotel front desk, and Mai's shop has been slow, so I keep checking its accounts at midnight.
This week I did three stupid things. I booked two families into the same room at the hotel, and the manager had to sort it out. I wrote my roll number wrong on Monday's accounts paper and had to run to the exam office. And yesterday I put sugar in the dal instead of salt. Mai, my mother, laughed, but I didn't.
I'm not careless, you know me. It's like my head is full and every new thing spills out.
Write when you can.
Samir

qa.q: What happened at the hotel this week?
qa.a: Samir booked two families into the same room, and the manager had to sort it out.

qa.q: How does Samir feel about the mistakes?
qa.a: Samir feels frustrated and a little scared, insisting "I'm not careless" while describing a head so full that new things spill out.

qa.q: What small step could Samir take to lighten the load during exams?
qa.a: Samir could ask the hotel for fewer shifts this month and pick one fixed time to check the shop accounts instead of every midnight, freeing some room in a crowded mind.

qa.q: What might Mai have been thinking when she laughed at the sweet dal?
qa.a: She probably laughed to ease the moment, but may also have noticed how stretched and tired Samir is, and felt worried.

grounding: A student juggling exams, a job and family worries writes about careless mistakes and a foggy, overfull mind.

passage: Lakshmi, you asked what that November was like. Honestly? Fog. I had semester exams, four online tutoring sessions a night to help at home since Baba lost his job, and a head full of "what if we can't pay the hostel fee". I thought I was managing. Then the mistakes started. I uploaded my cousin's birthday video instead of my lab report. In the circuits quiz I wrote milliamps where it should have been amps, on every single answer. One night I taught a Class 8 boy the wrong formula for area, and his mother messaged me the next day. I'm Bidisha, the girl who used to find everyone else's errors. That November I couldn't find my own. It wasn't that I didn't know the stuff. There just wasn't room left in my head.

qa.q: What did Bidisha upload instead of the lab report?
qa.a: Her cousin's birthday video.

qa.q: Why does Bidisha say it wasn't that she didn't know the stuff?
qa.a: She knew the material, but worry about money and too many jobs filled her mind, so there was no room left to catch errors 😔

qa.q: What could Bidisha have tried that November to clear some of the fog?
qa.a: She could have spoken to her tutor or a college counsellor about the pressure, dropped a tutoring session or two during exams, and used a short checklist before submitting work.

qa.q: How might the mother of the Class 8 boy see Bidisha's mistake?
qa.a: She would likely be worried about her son's homework and may have doubted the tutor, without knowing how stretched Bidisha was.

grounding: A student recalls how exams, night work and money worries used up her mental space and led to careless mistakes.

passage:
Monday: Seema, twenty-four, was coordinating her first big wedding for an events company in Jaipur. By noon she had eleven chat groups pinging, a florist on hold and the caterer's list in her head. She forgot to confirm the band. Jomon, the senior planner, had to call them himself.
Wednesday: Before switching on her phone, Seema wrote everything on one sheet. She broke the wedding into steps: venue, food, flowers, music, guests. She muted every group except the family's, and set a timer: fifty minutes of work, then ten minutes' walk on the terrace.
Saturday, the wedding: When the bride's aunt rushed up with a last-minute change, Seema jotted it on her sheet, finished the seating call, then handled it. Jomon found her calm by the gate at nine, ticking the last line.

qa.q: What did Seema forget on Monday?
qa.a: She forgot to confirm the band.

qa.q: What does Seema's calm at the gate on Saturday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt in control, because the jobs were on paper and in steps instead of all spinning in her head.

qa.q: Which change on Wednesday made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Writing everything on one sheet and muting all but one group, which freed her mind from remembering and from constant pings so she could focus.

qa.q: How might Jomon see Seema's change from Monday to Saturday?
qa.a: Jomon likely felt relieved and impressed, going from making her calls himself to watching her handle a last-minute change calmly 🙂

grounding: A young worker lightens her mental load by writing things down, breaking a big job into steps, muting needless alerts and taking breaks.

passage: Jasleen, you've got thirty tabs open and your phone keeps buzzing. Let your Alka Bua tell you something. When I was twenty-five, I worked as an assistant in a busy textile export office in Ludhiana. I kept everything in my head: orders, shipping dates, which buyer wanted which dye. One day I sent a whole consignment of blue fabric to the buyer who had ordered green. My boss didn't shout. She just handed me a fat register and said, "Your head is for thinking, not storing." So I learned. Every task went into the register. Big orders I broke into small steps. I stopped jumping at the office phone every time it rang and called back in batches. After lunch I walked round the block. I made fewer mistakes, and I went home less tired. So close those tabs, beta. Write it down.

qa.q: What mistake did young Alka make with the consignment?
qa.a: She sent a whole consignment of blue fabric to the buyer who had ordered green.

qa.q: What might young Alka have felt when her boss handed her the register?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed about the mistake but also relieved that her boss offered a way forward instead of shouting.

qa.q: Which of Alka's habits could help Jasleen most right now, and why?
qa.a: Writing every task down and answering calls in batches, because Jasleen's thirty tabs and buzzing phone are filling the mind the way Alka's once did.

qa.q: What might Jasleen feel hearing this from Alka Bua?
qa.a: Jasleen might feel understood rather than scolded, and more willing to close the tabs because someone who made the same mistakes is sharing what worked.

grounding: An aunt recalls how, as a young worker, she learned to write things down, break jobs into steps, batch interruptions and take breaks.

passage: At the branch post office in Chail, a village above Solan, Tanuja started on Monday as the new clerk. By noon Nikita, who had run the counter for six years, saw her staring at three registers, the money order forms and a queue of farmers, her pen frozen. Nikita had once handed the whole job to a newcomer at once and watched her quit within a week. So she closed the counter for ten minutes. "Today, only speed post. Nothing else." She did two bookings slowly while Tanuja watched, then let her do the next five with a small checklist taped beside the scale: weigh, stamp, enter, receipt. On Thursday they added money orders. By the next Monday Tanuja was handling the queue while Nikita sipped tea and watched, stepping in only once.

qa.q: What was on the checklist taped beside the scale?
qa.a: Weigh, stamp, enter, receipt.

qa.q: Why did Nikita close the counter for ten minutes?
qa.a: She saw Tanuja overwhelmed and remembered a newcomer who quit after getting everything at once, so she wanted to slow things down before Tanuja sank.

qa.q: Which step in Nikita's approach helped most, and why?
qa.a: Teaching only speed post first, with an example and a checklist; one small stage at a time let Tanuja practise before money orders were added.

qa.q: What might that first Monday noon have felt like for Tanuja?
qa.a: She likely felt frozen and panicky, with registers, forms and a waiting queue all demanding attention at once 😰

grounding: A senior clerk sees a new hire drowning in information and teaches the job in small stages with an example, a checklist and practice time.

passage: In the kitchen of a busy tapas bar in Seville, Jamal's first shift was a blur. The head cook had rattled off forty dishes, six fridge sections, the allergy rules and the order screen in five minutes. By eight, Jamal was holding a pan of garlic prawns and asking where the prawns were kept. Pablo, who had cooked there for three years, noticed Jamal's hands shaking. He pulled him aside. "Forget the forty dishes. Tonight you do three: the potatoes, the peppers, the tortilla." He made one tortilla slowly while Jamal watched, then taped a small card above Jamal's station with the three dishes and their steps. By Friday they added the prawns. Two weeks later Jamal was running the cold station and teaching the next newcomer with a card of his own.

qa.q: Which three dishes did Pablo give Jamal for the first night?
qa.a: The potatoes, the peppers, the tortilla.

qa.q: What did Jamal's shaking hands suggest to Pablo?
qa.a: They suggested Jamal was overwhelmed and anxious after being given forty dishes and rules in five minutes, far too much to take in at once.

qa.q: Which choice by Pablo turned Jamal's first week around, and why?
qa.a: Cutting the job to three dishes, showing one slowly and taping up a step card; small stages with an example and practice let Jamal learn without drowning.

qa.q: How might the next newcomer feel receiving a card from Jamal?
qa.a: The newcomer would probably feel relieved and supported, getting a manageable start from someone who clearly remembers being lost.

grounding: A senior cook notices a new hire overloaded with information and teaches in small stages, with a demonstration, a checklist card and practice.

passage: In their Bhopal flat, two-year-old Rayyan sat on the rug, pushing a yellow truck under the sofa and pulling it out again. "Rayyan! Lunch!" Zeenat called from the kitchen. He didn't look up. Dilnaz, his big sister, rolled her eyes. "He's ignoring you, Ammi." Zeenat came over, knelt beside him and touched his shoulder. Rayyan looked up, blinked, and smiled as if seeing her for the first time. "Truck," he said, holding it out.

qa.q: What was Rayyan doing with the yellow truck?
qa.a: Pushing it under the sofa and pulling it out again.

qa.q: What does Rayyan's smile, as if seeing Zeenat for the first time, suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he truly hadn't heard her; his attention was so full of the truck that her voice didn't get through, not that he was ignoring her.

qa.q: What did Zeenat do that worked better than calling louder?
qa.a: She came over, knelt beside him and touched his shoulder, which gently brought his attention from the truck to her.

qa.q: Why might Dilnaz think Rayyan was ignoring Ammi?
qa.a: From an older child's view, not answering looks like choosing not to listen, so Dilnaz reads it as defiance rather than a toddler's absorbed attention.

grounding: A toddler boy absorbed in his truck does not hear his mother call, a normal limit of attention that his sister mistakes for defiance.

passage:
"Advait! Shoes on, we're going to the park!"
Advait, two, didn't move. He was dropping pebbles into a steel glass, one by one.
"See, Trisha?" said Deepika, his Masi. "He's being stubborn."
"I don't think so, Didi. Watch." Trisha, his mother, crouched until her face was near the glass. "Clink," she said softly.
Advait looked up. "Clink!"
"One more clink, then shoes?"
He dropped a pebble, grinned, and held out his foot.
"So he just didn't hear?" said Deepika.
"His whole head was in that glass."

qa.q: What was Advait dropping into the steel glass?
qa.a: Pebbles, one by one.

qa.q: Why didn't Advait respond when he was called?
qa.a: His attention was completely on the pebbles and the glass, so the call didn't reach him; it wasn't stubbornness.

qa.q: What did Trisha do that got Advait's attention, and why did it work?
qa.a: She crouched near the glass and joined his game with a soft "clink", meeting his focus first and then gently turning it to shoes.

qa.q: How does Deepika's view of Advait change during the scene?
qa.a: She starts out thinking he is being stubborn, then sees he simply didn't hear because he was absorbed.

grounding: A toddler boy absorbed in dropping pebbles does not hear his name, and his mother shows it is a limit of attention, not defiance.

passage:
"Darshan, did you like the puppet show?"
"Yes, Dadu! The king puppet fell off the horse, and the horse danced!"
"Did you see Mama walk right past you in the middle of it? She was carrying the ice cream."
"No! Mama didn't come."
"She did. She walked in front of the stage and waved."
Darshan frowned. "I was watching the king. I didn't see anything else."
Dadu laughed. "That's how eyes work, little one. When you look hard at one thing, the rest goes away."
"Where's my ice cream, then?"
"Melting, in Mama's hand. Run!"

qa.q: What happened to the king puppet?
qa.a: The king puppet fell off the horse.

qa.q: Why was Darshan so sure Mama hadn't come?
qa.a: Darshan was so focused on the king puppet that nothing else got noticed, so it truly felt as if Mama was never there.

qa.q: How did Dadu handle Darshan's surprise, and why was that helpful?
qa.a: He laughed kindly and explained that looking hard at one thing makes the rest go away, so Darshan learned it was normal, not a silly mistake.

qa.q: What might Mama have felt when she waved and got no response?
qa.a: She may have been amused, seeing how completely the show had caught Darshan's attention even as she walked in front of the stage.

grounding: A preschooler watching a puppet show misses Mama walking right past, because attention locks onto one focus.

passage:
Teacher's note, KG-A, Friday. Payal
A puppet group visited today. During the story of the clever crow, our principal slowly crossed the back of the hall carrying a tall plant in a red pot. Afterwards I asked Indu, who sat in front, "Did anyone walk past during the show?" Indu said firmly, "No, Ma'am. Only the crow." When I told the class about the principal, Indu's eyes went round. "A PLANT? I didn't see!"
What I did next: we talked about how our eyes follow whatever our mind is busy with. Everyone giggled 😊

qa.q: What was the principal carrying across the hall?
qa.a: A tall plant in a red pot.

qa.q: What do Indu's round eyes suggest when hearing about the principal?
qa.a: They suggest real surprise; Indu had been so wrapped up in the crow that the principal simply wasn't seen.

qa.q: How did Payal turn the surprise into something useful for the class?
qa.a: She talked with them about how eyes follow whatever the mind is busy with, so missing the plant felt interesting rather than embarrassing.

qa.q: What might the principal have thought, walking across and seeing no heads turn?
qa.a: The principal may have been amused, seeing how completely the puppets held the children's attention.

grounding: A teacher notes a preschooler so absorbed in a puppet show that a person crossing the hall with a plant goes unseen.

passage:
"Lokesh, count how many times the white team passes the ball. Ready?" Shankar Thatha held up his phone.
"Easy." Lokesh leaned in, lips moving. "...fourteen, fifteen, sixteen! Sixteen!"
"Correct. And did you see the bear?"
"What bear?"
"Watch again. Don't count this time."
Lokesh watched. Halfway through, a person in a big brown bear costume walked into the middle of the players, waved and walked out.
"No way! That wasn't there before!"
"Same video, kanna."
"But I was looking right at the screen!"
"Your eyes were. Your mind was busy counting passes. What the mind is busy with decides what you see."
"Play it again. I want to show Amma. She'll never spot it."

qa.q: How many passes did Lokesh count?
qa.a: Sixteen.

qa.q: Why was Lokesh so sure the bear wasn't there the first time?
qa.a: Lokesh had been looking right at the screen, so missing something that big felt impossible; counting had taken up all of Lokesh's attention.

qa.q: What did Shankar Thatha do that helped Lokesh understand, and why did it work?
qa.a: He played the same video again without the counting task, so Lokesh could see directly that attention, not the eyes alone, decided what was noticed.

qa.q: What might Shankar Thatha enjoy about watching Lokesh's reaction?
qa.a: He likely enjoys the surprise on Lokesh's face and the chance to teach something memorable without a lecture.

grounding: A child counting passes in a video completely misses a person in a bear costume, showing that attention decides what is seen.

passage: I'm Ankita, and last week I learned my eyes can fool me. In computer class, Jyoti Ma'am played a short video of children passing a football. "Count the passes by the yellow shirts," she said. I counted so hard my finger tapped the desk: twenty-two. I was right! Then Ma'am asked, "Who saw the tiger?" Half the class put up their hands. I laughed, because I thought they were joking. She played it again. A person in a big orange tiger suit walked slowly across the field, stopped, did a little dance and left. I felt my face go hot. How did I miss a dancing tiger? Ma'am said, "You were busy counting. Your mind chose." Now I try the same trick on Papa at home.

qa.q: How many passes did Ankita count?
qa.a: Twenty-two.

qa.q: Why did Ankita's face go hot?
qa.a: Ankita felt embarrassed and surprised after laughing at the others, and then seeing that a dancing tiger had been there all along.

qa.q: What could Ankita try the next time a task needs full attention but the whole scene matters too?
qa.a: Ankita could remember that focus hides other things and, after finishing, look again at the whole scene or ask what else was there.

qa.q: How might the classmates who saw the tiger feel when Ankita laughed?
qa.a: They might have felt a bit brushed off at first, then pleased when the replay proved them right.

grounding: A child counting passes misses a person in a tiger suit crossing the screen, learning that attention, not the eyes alone, decides what is seen.
